Compares a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell in at least four features

topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an electron micrograph, can they tell whether it shows a bacterium or a plant cell and argue why mitochondria were once bacteria?

The bacterial cell was met in Sek I as a pathogen

topics.laenderNotes: NRW G9 Einführungsphase (Kl. 11) Inhaltsfeld Zellbiologie; in G8 Länder this is taught in Kl. 10 (E-Phase).

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Fluid Mosaic Model of Membranes
topics.description: Pupils explain the phospholipid bilayer with embedded and peripheral proteins and glycocalyx, and trace how the model developed from the Sandwich-Modell to the Flüssig-Mosaik-Modell as new methods (freeze fracture, cell fusion experiment) produced new evidence.
evidence: Draws and labels the fluid mosaic model with phospholipids, integral and peripheral proteins and glycocalyx
Explains bilayer formation from the hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails of phospholipids
Describes an experiment that refuted the sandwich model and what it showed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees results of the mouse–human cell fusion experiment, can they explain what it shows about how membranes are built?

prerequisites.reason: Membranes create the compartments
Hydrophilic/hydrophobic behaviour rests on intermolecular forces

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Diffusion and Osmosis
topics.description: Pupils explain diffusion as net particle movement down a concentration gradient and osmosis as water movement through a selectively permeable membrane, and use plasmolysis and deplasmolysis to show why cells need a stable osmotic value (Homöostase).
evidence: Predicts whether a red onion cell will plasmolyse in a given salt solution and explains why
Interprets data from a potato-cylinder or egg osmosis experiment
Explains why drinking sea water dehydrates the body
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} puts red onion cells into strong salt water, can they predict what they will see under the microscope and explain it?

prerequisites.reason: Osmosis needs a selectively permeable membrane
Diffusion is explained by particle motion

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Membrane Transport: Channels, Carriers and Pumps
topics.description: Pupils distinguish passive transport (simple diffusion, channels, carriers) from active transport against a gradient (Na⁺/K⁺-Pumpe using ATP) and bulk transport by endo- and exocytosis, and relate each to examples.
evidence: Sorts transport examples into passive, facilitated and active transport and justifies the choice
Explains why the sodium–potassium pump needs ATP
Interprets a graph of uptake rate against concentration for channel- versus carrier-mediated transport
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that a poison blocks ATP production, can they predict which membrane transport processes stop and which carry on?

prerequisites.reason: Active transport is defined in contrast to diffusion
Channels and carriers are membrane proteins

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Protein Structure and Function
topics.description: Pupils describe how amino acids join by peptide bonds and fold into primary to quaternary structure, and explain the lock-and-key relation between a protein's 3D shape and its function (enzyme, receptor, transporter, antibody); denaturation destroys function.
evidence: Explains the four levels of protein structure with the bonds that hold each level
Gives three protein functions with an example each
Explains why heating or a strong acid makes a protein lose its function
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} fries an egg, can they explain at molecular level why the egg white turns solid and can no longer function as before?

prerequisites.reason: Amino acids as building blocks were met in Sek I
Folding is held by hydrogen bonds and other intermolecular forces

topics.laenderNotes: NRW EF (Biochemie der Zelle); Bayern treats biomolecules in Biologie 10 and Chemie 11.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Cell Differentiation and Stem Cells
topics.description: Pupils explain how all body cells carry the same genes but differentiate by switching genes on and off, distinguish embryonic, adult and induced pluripotent stem cells, and weigh arguments in the German debate on embryonic stem cell research (Stammzellgesetz).
evidence: Explains totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent with examples
Describes one medical use of stem cells and its current limits
Separates descriptive and normative statements in a text on embryonic stem cell research
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that a lab grew heart muscle from skin cells, can they explain what kind of stem cells were used and why this matters ethically?

prerequisites.reason: Differentiation underlies division of labour in multicellular organisms
The stem cell debate is evaluated with the bioethics procedure
Stem cells renew by mitosis

osMatches.note: os combines cancer and stem cells at age 13-14

topics.laenderNotes: The legal frame (Stammzellgesetz, Embryonenschutzgesetz) is German-specific; NRW EF names the embryonic stem cell debate explicitly.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Photosynthesis and Cell Respiration Compared
topics.description: Pupils write both processes as word equations (later with formulas), state where they happen (Chloroplast, Mitochondrium), test predictions with classic experiments (starch test, oxygen from Wasserpest) and explain why plants respire day and night while they photosynthesise only in light.

Plans an experiment on light dependence with a control, e.g. starch test on half-covered leaves
Explains the overall gas exchange of a plant by day and by night

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the Kl. 6 introduction to photosynthesis
Chloroplasts and mitochondria are the sites of the two processes
Experiments need controls and variable control

topics.laenderNotes: BW 7/8, NRW IF4 (typically Kl. 7 or 8), Berlin/Brandenburg 7/8; Bayern treats cell respiration in Biologie 10.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: How Enzymes Work
topics.description: Pupils explain enzymes as proteins that speed up reactions without being used up, using the lock-and-key model (aktives Zentrum, Substratspezifität), and show experimentally (e.g. amylase and starch) that enzyme activity depends on temperature and pH.
evidence: Explains substrate specificity with the lock-and-key model
Plans and evaluates an amylase–starch experiment with iodine and a control
Explains with a graph why enzyme activity drops sharply above about 40 °C
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} chews a piece of bread for a long time and it tastes sweet, can they explain which enzyme is at work and why boiling would stop it?

prerequisites.reason: Digestion is where enzymes are first met
Enzyme experiments test hypotheses with controls

osMatches.note: os names enzymes as catalysts within digestion

topics.laenderNotes: BW 7/8, Bayern Biologie 10, NRW Kl. 5/6 (model only) and EF (kinetics).

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Fermentation: Energy Without Oxygen
topics.description: Pupils compare cell respiration with alcoholic fermentation (Hefe: Brot, Bier) and lactic acid fermentation (Joghurt, Sauerkraut, sprinting muscles) as reaction schemes and energy yields, and connect them to food biotechnology.
evidence: Writes reaction schemes for alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation
Explains with an experiment why bread dough rises
States that fermentation yields far less energy than respiration and explains what this means for a sprinter
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} bakes bread with yeast, can they explain where the bubbles come from and why yeast without oxygen grows more slowly?

prerequisites.reason: Fermentation is defined against aerobic respiration
Fermentation pathways are enzyme-driven

osMatches.note: os focuses on lactic acid in muscles; German adds yeast fermentation

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: microorganisms in biotechnology (Biologie 9) and muscle metabolism (Biologie 10); KMK lists fermentation in detail only for eA in the Abitur.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Enzyme Kinetics and Inhibition
topics.description: Pupils read saturation curves (rate against substrate concentration, vmax, qualitative Km), explain temperature (RGT rule, denaturation) and pH optima, and distinguish competitive, non-competitive/allosteric inhibition and end-product inhibition as ways cells regulate metabolism.
evidence: Interprets a saturation curve and explains why it levels off
Distinguishes competitive from allosteric inhibition by how extra substrate changes the curve
Explains end-product inhibition as negative feedback in a metabolic pathway
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees two enzyme curves, one recovering with more substrate and one not, can they say which inhibitor type each shows and why?

prerequisites.reason: Deepens the Sek I enzyme model
Enzyme shape follows from protein structure

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: reading and interpreting graphs of functions (saturation curves, limits)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Saturation curves are function graphs

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: ATP and Energy Coupling
topics.description: Pupils explain ATP as the universal, short-term energy carrier that couples energy-releasing (catabolic) to energy-consuming (anabolic) reactions, and NAD⁺/NADH and NADP⁺/NADPH as redox carriers linking the pathways.
evidence: Explains energy coupling with an example such as muscle contraction or active transport
Describes ATP hydrolysis and regeneration as a cycle
Distinguishes anabolic and catabolic pathways and assigns photosynthesis and respiration
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that the body turns over roughly its own weight in ATP each day, can they explain how that is possible with only a few grams stored?

prerequisites.reason: The two processes are now seen as linked anabolism and catabolism
Redox carriers require the electron-transfer view of redox

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Chloroplasts, Pigments and Spectra
topics.description: Pupils relate leaf and chloroplast structure (thylakoids, stroma) to function, separate leaf pigments by chromatography, and compare the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll with the action spectrum of photosynthesis (Engelmann experiment).
evidence: Separates leaf pigments by thin-layer or paper chromatography and identifies the bands
Explains why the action and absorption spectra are similar but not identical
Interprets the Engelmann bacteria experiment
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} grows plants under green light only, can they predict and explain how well the plants will grow?

prerequisites.reason: Revisits leaf tissues as functional adaptations
Thylakoids and stroma are compartments

externalPrerequisites.subject: Physik
externalPrerequisites.concept: visible light spectrum and colour (wavelength)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Spectra are read against wavelength

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Limiting Factors of Photosynthesis
topics.description: Pupils analyse how light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature limit the rate of photosynthesis (Minimumprinzip, compensation point), compare sun and shade leaves, and apply this to greenhouse farming.
evidence: Identifies the limiting factor at different points of a light–rate curve
Explains the light compensation point and how it differs for sun and shade leaves
Justifies why greenhouse growers add CO₂ and heat in winter
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that a greenhouse plant grows no faster with more light, can they suggest what else is limiting and how to test it?

prerequisites.reason: Quantifies the light dependence met in Sek I
Light capture by pigments explains light limitation

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Light-Dependent Reactions
topics.description: Pupils explain how photosystems in the thylakoid membrane use light to split water (Fotolyse), drive an electron transport chain, build up a proton gradient and make ATP by chemiosmosis and NADPH, and how these products feed the Calvin cycle.
evidence: Describes the path of electrons from water to NADP⁺ and names the by-product oxygen
Explains chemiosmotic ATP synthesis via the proton gradient and ATP synthase
Explains why the Calvin cycle stops soon after the light is switched off
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told that the oxygen we breathe comes from water rather than from CO₂, can they explain which reaction step shows this?

prerequisites.reason: Pigments in the thylakoids capture the light
ATP and NADPH are the products of the light reactions

topics.laenderNotes: The energy model of the light reactions (Z-Schema) and the light-harvesting complex are eA only (KMK 2020).

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Calvin Cycle
topics.description: Pupils describe the three phases of the Calvin cycle (fixation of CO₂ by RuBisCO, reduction with ATP and NADPH, regeneration of ribulose bisphosphate), its carbon balance, and how tracer experiments with ¹⁴C revealed it.
evidence: Names and explains the three phases with the role of ATP and NADPH
Calculates how many turns of the cycle are needed for one glucose molecule
Interprets a ¹⁴C tracer experiment that identified the first stable product
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees data that radioactive carbon first appears in a three-carbon compound, can they explain what this tells us about CO₂ fixation?

prerequisites.reason: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: C4 and CAM Plants
topics.description: Pupils explain how C4 plants (maize) separate CO₂ pre-fixation and the Calvin cycle in space and CAM plants (cacti) in time, and why this is an adaptation to hot, dry habitats.
evidence: Compares C3, C4 and CAM plants in a table (where and when CO₂ is fixed)
Explains why C4 plants can photosynthesise with nearly closed stomata
Predicts which plant type wins at high temperature and low CO₂
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that maize outgrows wheat in hot summers, can they explain the biochemical reason?

prerequisites.reason: C4 metabolism adds a step before the Calvin cycle
Explains differences in limiting factors

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Glycolysis and the Citric Acid Cycle
topics.description: Pupils follow glucose through glycolysis in the cytoplasm, oxidative decarboxylation and the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and draw up the balance of ATP, NADH/FADH₂ and CO₂ for each step.
evidence: States where each step happens and what goes in and comes out
Draws up the balance of ATP and reduced carriers per glucose up to the citric acid cycle
Explains why the carbon atoms of glucose leave the body as CO₂ in the breath
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked where the carbon of a slice of bread ends up after cell respiration, can they trace it step by step?

prerequisites.reason: The pathway is balanced in ATP and redox carriers
Steps take place in different compartments

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Respiratory Chain and ATP Synthase
topics.description: Pupils explain how NADH and FADH₂ deliver electrons to the respiratory chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane, how the resulting proton gradient drives ATP synthase, why oxygen is the final electron acceptor, and how poisons (cyanide) or uncouplers act.
evidence: Explains the role of oxygen as final electron acceptor and the formation of water
Compares chemiosmotic ATP synthesis in mitochondria and chloroplasts
Predicts the effect of a respiratory poison or an uncoupler on ATP yield and body temperature
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that cyanide blocks the last enzyme of the respiratory chain, can they explain why this is fatal within minutes?

prerequisites.reason: The respiratory chain oxidises the carriers produced earlier
Chemiosmosis was introduced for the chloroplast

topics.laenderNotes: The energy model of the respiratory chain and fermentation pathways in detail are eA only (KMK 2020).

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Hypothesis-Driven Experiments with Controls
topics.description: Pupils move from fair tests to the full scientific cycle in biology: they state a cause–effect hypothesis, name independent and dependent variables, set up a control, collect data (also with digital sensors) and decide whether the data support or refute the hypothesis.
evidence: Writes a testable hypothesis in "If …, then …" form for a biological question
Designs an experiment with one changed variable, constants and a control
States from the results whether the hypothesis is supported and names one source of error
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to know whether cress germinates better in light, can they plan an experiment that would convince a sceptic?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on controlling variables from Kl. 5/6
Extends the scientific method cycle

topics.laenderNotes: Taught in every Land through content topics rather than as a separate unit.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Using and Judging Models in Biology
topics.nameDe: Modelle in der Biologie nutzen und beurteilen
topics.description: Pupils distinguish structural models (Herzmodell), functional models (Lungenmodell) and thought models (Schlüssel-Schloss-Modell), test predictions derived from a model, and say where a model fits the original and where it fails.
evidence: Classifies three biology models as structural, functional or thought model
Names two ways a given model matches and two ways it differs from reality
Derives a testable prediction from a model and says how to check it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses the balloon model of the lungs, can they explain what it shows well and what it gets wrong about real breathing?

prerequisites.reason: Model predictions are tested experimentally
Familiar body models serve as examples

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Proximate and Ultimate Explanations
topics.description: Pupils distinguish "how" explanations (mechanism, proximate) from "why did it evolve" explanations (fitness advantage, ultimate) and avoid purpose language such as "the giraffe grew a long neck in order to…" (finale Erklärungen).
evidence: Gives a proximate and an ultimate explanation for the same phenomenon, e.g. birdsong
Rewrites a teleological sentence into a scientifically correct one
Spots the explanation type in three given statements
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears "cacti have spines so that animals don't eat them", can they say what is wrong and reformulate it correctly?

prerequisites.reason: Different kinds of explanation are part of thinking about scientific knowledge
Adaptations of animals offer the examples

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Ethical Decision-Making in Biology
topics.description: Pupils follow a structured evaluation procedure on biology dilemmas (organ donation, genetic testing, GM crops): separate descriptive from normative statements, identify values, weigh criteria and options, decide, and reflect on consequences and the process.
evidence: Marks descriptive and normative statements in a short text and names the value behind a normative one
Weighs at least three criteria for two options and reaches a justified decision
Reflects on short- and long-term consequences of the decision for individuals and society
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} discusses whether everyone should be an organ donor unless they object, can they separate facts from values and argue their position step by step?

A reasoned statement is the written form of the judgement

externalPrerequisites.subject: Religion & Ethik
externalPrerequisites.concept: ethical argument types (consequentialist and duty-based reasoning)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Ethical frameworks help weigh normative arguments

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: How Biological Knowledge Is Made
topics.description: Pupils reflect on criteria of scientific knowledge (evidence, theory, falsifiability, peer review, reproducibility), on what a "theory" means in science, and on how new methods (electron microscopy, sequencing) changed biological models.
evidence: Explains the difference between a hypothesis, a theory and an everyday "theory"
Describes how a model was revised after new evidence, e.g. the membrane model
Judges whether a claim in the media is backed by scientific evidence and peer review
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears "evolution is only a theory", can they explain what a scientific theory is and why that sentence is misleading?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on judging models
Reflects on the hypothesis–experiment cycle

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Nutrients and Their Building Blocks
topics.description: Pupils describe carbohydrates (mono-, di- and polysaccharides), fats (glycerol and fatty acids) and proteins (amino acids) with simple models, detect them with standard tests (iodine, Fehling or glucose strips, grease spot, biuret) and explain their roles as fuel and building material.

topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} tests a crisp, a slice of apple and a piece of cheese, can they predict and check which nutrients each contains?

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Enzymatic Digestion and Absorption
topics.description: Pupils follow each nutrient through mouth, stomach and small intestine, name the digestive enzymes and their products, and explain how villi and microvilli enlarge the surface so that building blocks pass into the blood (Oberflächenvergrößerung).

Explains why undigested starch cannot pass into the blood

Digestive enzymes do the breaking down
Revisits the digestive organs from Kl. 6

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Bacteria and Viruses as Pathogens
topics.description: Pupils compare the structure and reproduction of bacteria (prokaryotic cell, binary fission, exponential growth) and viruses (protein coat, nucleic acid, multiplication only inside host cells), describe the course of an infection and explain how hygiene breaks infection chains.

Describes the stages of an infectious disease from infection to recovery
Explains with an agar-plate experiment why hand-washing reduces infections
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a cold, can they explain why antibiotics will not help and how the virus spreads to others?

Builds on hygiene habits from primary school

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Innate Immune Defence

Explains redness, swelling and warmth of an inflamed cut
Describes phagocytosis by a macrophage step by step

topics.name: Adaptive Immune Response

topics.name: Vaccination: Active and Passive Immunisation

Explains herd immunity with a simple model or simulation

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Antibiotics and Resistance

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle

Uses the principle of hormone action

topics.name: Contraception and the Pearl Index

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Sexual Diversity, Relationships and Consent

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Abortion Debate

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Stimulus, Response and Reflexes

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Neurons and Synapses: A First Model

prerequisites.reason: Neurons carry the signals in the stimulus–response chain
The neuron is a specialised cell

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Eye and Vision
topics.nameDe: Das Auge: Bau, Akkommodation und Fehlsichtigkeit
topics.description: Pupils explain how cornea and lens focus light on the retina, how the lens adjusts for near and far (Akkommodation), how rods and cones turn light into nerve signals, and how glasses correct short- and long-sightedness.
evidence: Labels the parts of the eye and gives their functions
Explains accommodation for a near and a far object
Explains with a ray diagram which lens corrects short-sightedness
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} cannot read the board but can read a book easily, can they explain what is wrong with the eye and what kind of lens helps?

prerequisites.reason: The eye is a sense organ in the stimulus–response chain
Seeing needs light travelling into the eye

externalPrerequisites.subject: Physik
externalPrerequisites.concept: converging and diverging lenses and image formation
externalPrerequisites.reason: Focusing and correction rely on lens optics

osMatches.note: os age 7-9 without accommodation and defects of vision

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Biologie 8 and BW 7/8; not explicit in NRW Biologie (lenses are in Physik).

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: How Hormones Work
topics.description: Pupils explain that endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, that only target cells with matching receptors respond (Schlüssel-Schloss-Prinzip), and compare hormonal with nervous signalling in speed, duration and reach.

Explains with the lock-and-key model why a hormone acts only on certain cells
Compares nerves and hormones in a table (speed, path, duration)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that adrenaline reaches every cell but speeds up only some, can they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Hormones are compared with nervous signalling
Hormones travel in the blood

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Blood Sugar Regulation and Diabetes
topics.description: Pupils explain blood sugar control as a feedback loop with the antagonists insulin and glucagon, and compare causes, effects and treatment of type 1 and type 2 diabetes, including prevention through lifestyle.
evidence: Draws the blood sugar control loop with sensor, regulator, effectors and negative feedback
Interprets a glucose tolerance curve of a healthy and a diabetic person
Compares type 1 and type 2 diabetes in cause and treatment
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees blood sugar values after a meal for two people, can they tell which one may have diabetes and explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Insulin and glucagon are hormones
Glucose comes from carbohydrate digestion

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Stress Response
topics.description: Pupils explain the fight-or-flight response as the joint action of the sympathetic nervous system and the hormones adrenaline and cortisol, contrast it with the calming parasympathetic system, and judge the health effects of long-term stress and ways to cope.
evidence: Describes three body changes in an acute stress situation and their purpose
Explains the roles of sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system
Suggests and justifies two strategies against chronic exam stress
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s heart races before a test, can they explain which systems cause this and why it was useful for our ancestors?

prerequisites.reason: Stress hormones act together with nerves
The nervous system triggers the fast part of the response

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Addiction and Drugs at the Synapse
topics.description: Pupils explain how nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and other drugs change transmission at synapses and the reward system, how tolerance and dependence develop, and evaluate prevention approaches, including behavioural addictions such as gaming.
evidence: Explains with a synapse model how a drug that mimics a transmitter changes signalling
Describes physical and psychological dependence and tolerance
Evaluates one prevention measure for young people
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that "one cigarette a day is harmless", can they explain why nicotine is addictive and what happens with regular use?

prerequisites.reason: Drugs act at synapses
Builds on smoking and addiction prevention from Kl. 6

osMatches.note: os age 13-14 without the synapse mechanism

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Biologie 8 (Suchtgefahren); the 2024 partial legalisation of cannabis in Germany is a frequent discussion context.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Resting Potential
topics.description: Pupils explain the resting potential of about −70 mV from unequal ion distribution, selective K⁺ permeability and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, and how it is measured with microelectrodes and an oscilloscope.
evidence: Explains how K⁺ outflow through leak channels creates a negative inside
Explains why the Na⁺/K⁺ pump is needed to maintain the potential
Predicts the effect of raising the outside K⁺ concentration on the membrane potential
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told the inside of a nerve cell is negative at rest, can they explain which ions and channels cause this?

prerequisites.reason: Ion channels and pumps are membrane transport
Revisits the neuron at membrane level

externalPrerequisites.subject: Physik
externalPrerequisites.concept: electric charge, potential difference and voltage
externalPrerequisites.reason: Membrane potentials are electrical voltages

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Action Potential
topics.description: Pupils explain the phases of an action potential (threshold, depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation) with voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels, the all-or-nothing principle, the refractory period and frequency coding of stimulus strength.
evidence: Labels the phases of an action potential curve and links each to channel states
Explains the all-or-nothing principle and how stimulus strength is coded
Explains why the refractory period limits firing frequency
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an oscilloscope trace of a stronger stimulus, can they explain why the spikes get more frequent but not taller?

prerequisites.reason: The action potential starts from the resting potential

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Continuous and Saltatory Conduction
topics.description: Pupils explain how action potentials spread along unmyelinated axons and jump between nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons, compare conduction speeds and relate demyelination (multiple sclerosis) to symptoms.
evidence: Explains why saltatory conduction is faster and saves energy
Compares conduction speed data for different axon types
Explains symptoms of multiple sclerosis from the loss of myelin
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that a squid has giant unmyelinated axons, can they explain how vertebrates achieve fast conduction differently?

prerequisites.reason: Conduction is the spread of action potentials

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Excitatory Chemical Synapse
topics.description: Pupils explain synaptic transmission in detail (Ca²⁺ influx, exocytosis, transmitter binding, ligand-gated channels, EPSP, transmitter breakdown by acetylcholinesterase) and the neuromuscular junction as the link to muscle contraction.
evidence: Describes the events at a cholinergic synapse in the correct order
Explains how frequency of action potentials is translated into transmitter amount
Explains the role of acetylcholinesterase and what happens if it is blocked
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a diagram of a synapse with a missing step, can they explain what goes wrong when calcium cannot enter?

prerequisites.reason: Action potentials arrive at the synapse
Deepens the Sek I synapse model

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Drugs and Toxins at Synapses
topics.description: Pupils explain how substances interfere with synapses at specific steps (blocking transmitter release like botulinum toxin, blocking receptors like curare, inhibiting the enzyme like nerve agents, acting as agonists like nicotine) and use this to predict effects of medicines and drugs.
evidence: Assigns given substances to the synaptic step they affect
Predicts muscle effects of a receptor blocker versus an esterase inhibitor
Explains how an antidote for a nerve-agent poisoning could work
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that Botox smooths wrinkles, can they explain at which step of the synapse it acts and why the muscle relaxes?

prerequisites.reason: Each substance targets a step of synaptic transmission
Revisits drug action from Sek I at molecular level

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Inhibitory Synapses and Summation
topics.description: Pupils explain IPSPs at inhibitory synapses and how a neuron integrates excitatory and inhibitory inputs by spatial and temporal summation at the axon hillock.
evidence: Explains how an inhibitory transmitter makes the membrane more negative
Predicts from given EPSPs and IPSPs whether the neuron fires
Distinguishes spatial and temporal summation with an example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees three inputs to a neuron, two excitatory and one inhibitory, can they work out whether an action potential is triggered?

prerequisites.reason: Inhibitory synapses are defined against excitatory ones

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Sensory Cells and the Receptor Potential
topics.description: Pupils explain how primary and secondary sensory cells transduce a stimulus into a graded receptor potential and then into action-potential frequency, using a mechanoreceptor or photoreceptor as example.
evidence: Distinguishes primary and secondary sensory cells with examples
Explains the relation between stimulus strength, receptor potential and AP frequency
Interprets recordings from a sensory cell
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a recording where a stronger touch produces a larger receptor potential, can they explain how this is passed on to the brain?

prerequisites.reason: Receptor potentials are coded as AP frequency
Photoreceptors were met in Sek I

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Neuronal Plasticity and Learning
topics.nameDe: Neuronale Plastizität und zelluläre Grundlagen des Lernens
topics.description: Pupils explain how synapses change with use (long-term potentiation, more receptors, new synapses), relate this to memory, and discuss disorders of the nervous system (Alzheimer, Parkinson) and the methods used to study the brain (EEG, fMRI).
evidence: Describes long-term potentiation as a cellular basis of learning
Explains one neurodegenerative disease at the level of neurons or transmitters
Says what an EEG and an fMRI scan can and cannot show
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} practises vocabulary every day, can they explain what changes at the synapses in their brain?

prerequisites.reason: Plasticity changes how inputs are integrated
Learning strengthens synapses

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Chromosomes, Genes and DNA
topics.description: Pupils explain that the nucleus holds the genetic information as DNA packed into chromosomes, describe the DNA double helix with complementary base pairs in a simple model, read a human karyogram (46 chromosomes, homologous pairs, autosomes, X and Y) and explain sex determination.
evidence: Explains the relation between DNA, gene and chromosome with a sketch
Builds or describes a simple DNA model with complementary base pairing
Reads a karyogram and determines the sex and the number of chromosomes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a human karyogram, can they say whether it is from a man or a woman and explain what the pairs mean?

prerequisites.reason: The nucleus holds the chromosomes
Inheritance starts with fertilisation

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Biologie 9, BW 9/10, NRW IF6 (Kl. 7–10, often 9), Berlin/Brandenburg 9/10.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Cell Cycle and Mitosis
topics.description: Pupils describe the cell cycle with DNA replication in interphase and the phases of mitosis, explain the change between one- and two-chromatid chromosomes, and why mitosis yields genetically identical cells for growth and repair.
evidence: Orders micrographs of a root tip into the phases of mitosis
Explains with a chromosome model why both daughter cells get the same information
Names three situations in the body where mitosis takes place
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a grazed knee that heals, can they explain which kind of cell division repairs the skin and why the new cells carry the same genes?

prerequisites.reason: Mitosis distributes chromosomes
Growth of multicellular organisms needs cell division

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Meiosis and Genetic Variation
topics.description: Pupils explain how meiosis halves the chromosome set to form gametes, how random distribution of homologous chromosomes (and crossing-over) creates new combinations, and compare meiosis with mitosis.
evidence: Explains why gametes must be haploid
Calculates the number of possible chromosome combinations for a given number of pairs
Compares meiosis and mitosis in purpose, number of divisions and result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders why siblings look different even with the same parents, can they explain it with meiosis and fertilisation?

prerequisites.reason: Meiosis is compared with mitosis
Counting combinations uses the multiplication principle

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: From Gene to Trait
topics.nameDe: Vom Gen zum Merkmal: Prinzip der Proteinbiosynthese
topics.description: Pupils describe the basic principle that the base sequence of a gene determines the amino-acid sequence of a protein, and that proteins (enzymes, structural and transport proteins) produce traits, using an example such as albinism or eye colour (Genwirkkette).
evidence: Explains in three steps how DNA information becomes a protein
Explains with an example how a missing enzyme leads to a visible trait
Names three types of proteins and their role in the body
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} meets a person with albinism, can they explain how a change in one gene can lead to light skin and hair?

prerequisites.reason: Genes are sections of DNA
Many gene products are enzymes

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Mendel's Rules of Inheritance
topics.description: Pupils apply the uniformity and segregation rules (and, in outline, independent assortment) to monohybrid crosses with dominant–recessive and intermediate inheritance, using genotype, phenotype and Punnett squares.
evidence: Solves a monohybrid cross with a Punnett square and states the expected ratios
Distinguishes genotype and phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous
Explains why observed ratios in small samples differ from expected ones
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} crosses two heterozygous pea plants, can they predict the ratio of flower colours in the offspring and explain it?

prerequisites.reason: Segregation of alleles happens in meiosis
Ratios are compared with observed frequencies

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: probabilities of combined events with tree diagrams
externalPrerequisites.reason: Cross outcomes are probabilities

topics.laenderNotes: NRW and BW name rules of inheritance explicitly; Bayern's Biologie 9 concentrates on molecular genetics and recombination.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Human Pedigree Analysis
topics.description: Pupils read and analyse family pedigrees to decide whether a trait is inherited dominantly or recessively and autosomally or X-linked (e.g. cystic fibrosis, red–green colour blindness, haemophilia), and give genotypes of family members.
evidence: Decides the mode of inheritance from a pedigree and justifies it with a key family
Assigns genotypes to all individuals of a given pedigree
Calculates the risk for a child of two carrier parents
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a pedigree where two healthy parents have an affected son, can they work out how the trait is inherited?

prerequisites.reason: Pedigrees apply the rules of inheritance to humans
X-linked inheritance needs the sex chromosomes

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Chromosome Mutations: Trisomy 21
topics.description: Pupils explain how non-disjunction in meiosis leads to an extra chromosome, identify trisomy 21 in a karyogram, describe its effects, and reflect on prenatal diagnosis and genetic counselling.
evidence: Explains non-disjunction with a meiosis diagram
Identifies trisomy 21 or another numerical anomaly in a karyogram
States what prenatal tests can show and names one ethical question they raise
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that the risk of trisomy 21 rises with the mother's age, can they explain where in meiosis the error happens?

prerequisites.reason: The error arises during meiosis
Karyograms show the chromosome set

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Genetic Engineering: Principles and Uses

Explains what "genetically modified organism" means and gives an example
Evaluates a GM crop with at least three criteria from different perspectives
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a supermarket label "ohne Gentechnik", can they explain what it means and discuss whether it matters?

prerequisites.reason: A transferred gene is expressed as a protein
Applications are evaluated ethically
Bacteria are the production organisms

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Biologie 9 and BW 9/10; NRW and the KMK Abitur standards treat methods (PCR, vectors) only in the Leistungskurs.

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: DNA Structure and Semiconservative Replication
topics.description: Pupils describe nucleotides, antiparallel strands and base pairing in detail and explain semiconservative replication with its enzymes (helicase, DNA polymerase, ligase, leading and lagging strand) and the Meselson–Stahl experiment as evidence.
evidence: Explains antiparallel orientation and why replication of the lagging strand is discontinuous
Interprets the bands of the Meselson–Stahl experiment after one and two generations

prerequisites.reason: Deepens the simple DNA model
Replication precedes cell division

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Transcription and RNA Processing

evidence: Writes the mRNA for a given template DNA strand
Explains why eukaryotic mRNA is shorter than its gene
Explains how alternative splicing lets one gene code for several proteins
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a DNA template strand, can they write the mRNA and explain what happens to it before it leaves the nucleus?

prerequisites.reason: Base pairing and strand direction are needed
Deepens the Sek I principle of protein synthesis

osMatches.note: os central dogma at concept level only

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Translation and the Genetic Code

evidence: Translates an mRNA sequence into amino acids using the code sun
Describes initiation, elongation and termination at the ribosome

osMatches.note: os central dogma at concept level only

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Gene Mutations and Their Effects

evidence: Predicts the effect of a substitution, insertion and deletion on a given sequence
Explains sickle-cell anaemia from DNA to symptoms
Explains why a frameshift is usually more harmful than a substitution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a DNA sequence with one base changed, can they work out whether the protein changes and how much?

prerequisites.reason: Effects are predicted with the genetic code

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Gene Regulation in Eukaryotes
topics.description: Pupils explain how transcription factors, enhancers and silencers switch genes on and off, so that different cell types express different genes, and how signals from outside (hormones) reach the genome.

Describes how a transcription factor binds and activates a gene
Interprets an experiment on gene expression in different tissues

Differentiation is the result of gene regulation

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Epigenetics: DNA Methylation

Distinguishes a mutation from an epigenetic change

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Genetic Testing, Counselling and Gene Therapy

Evaluates a predictive genetic test from the view of the person and the family

Diseases are traced to mutations
Tests and therapies are evaluated ethically

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Cancer: Oncogenes and Tumour Suppressors
topics.description: Pupils explain cancer as uncontrolled cell division after several mutations in proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes (e.g. p53), and describe how personalised medicine targets specific mutations.

Oncogenes control the cell cycle
Cancer is uncontrolled mitosis

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: PCR and Gel Electrophoresis

Interprets a gel to identify a suspect or a father

externalPrerequisites.concept: exponential growth and powers of 2

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Genetic Engineering Methods
topics.description: Pupils explain how restriction enzymes, ligase and plasmid vectors move genes into organisms, how CRISPR/Cas edits genes precisely, and how gene-therapy approaches use these tools; they evaluate risks and regulation.

Explains how the guide RNA directs Cas9 to its target
Evaluates germline editing versus somatic editing

Gene cloning uses PCR and gel analysis

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection
topics.description: Pupils explain evolution by natural selection from variation, overproduction, competition, differential reproduction and inheritance, contrast it with Lamarck's idea, and compare natural selection with artificial selection (Züchtung).

Compares breeding of dog breeds with natural selection

Breeding from wild forms was met in Kl. 5/6

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Biologie 9, BW 9/10, Berlin/Brandenburg 9/10, NRW IF5 (Kl. 7–10).

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Evidence for Evolution

Distinguishes homologous from analogous organs with examples
Explains what makes Archaeopteryx a transitional fossil
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a bird wing and a butterfly wing, can they say whether they are evidence for close relationship and why?

Comparing vertebrate classes provides homologies

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Species Concept and Speciation
topics.description: Pupils apply the biological species concept (reproductive community, fertile offspring) and explain how geographic isolation, mutation and selection can split one species into two, e.g. Darwin finches or Galápagos tortoises.
evidence: Applies the biological species concept to horse, donkey and mule
Explains allopatric speciation in steps with a diagram
Explains adaptive radiation using Darwin finches

Genetic variation arises by recombination

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Classification and Phylogenetic Trees
topics.description: Pupils place organisms in the hierarchy of the natural system (Reich, Stamm, Klasse, Ordnung, Familie, Gattung, Art), read phylogenetic trees as hypotheses of relatedness and relate the order of appearance of vertebrate groups to geological time.

Explains why a tree is a hypothesis that can change

Identification keys introduced ordering by features

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Human Evolution

Explains the Out-of-Africa model with evidence
Explains why human "races" are not a valid biological category

Fossils are the main evidence

topics.name: Synthetic Theory: Factors of Evolution

Explains genetic drift with a founder or bottleneck example
Distinguishes scientific and non-scientific explanations of the diversity of life by their criteria

Mutation is the source of new alleles
Distinguishing science from non-science
Creation stories are discussed alongside the scientific theory

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Population Genetics: Hardy–Weinberg

Explains what a deviation from expected genotype frequencies indicates
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that 1 in 2,500 newborns has cystic fibrosis, can they calculate roughly how many people are carriers?

Genotype frequencies come from allele combinations

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Isolation Mechanisms and Modes of Speciation

Explains sympatric speciation with an example

topics.subject: Biologie

Sequence differences are accumulated mutations

topics.subject: Biologie

Behaviour is explained ultimately

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Human Evolution and Cultural Evolution

Genetic evidence on human origins
Primate behaviour is analysed by fitness

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Ecosystem: Biotope and Community

topics.name: Measuring Abiotic Factors in the Field

Identifies typical species with a key or app and records where they occur
Relates the distribution of an indicator plant to a measured factor

Species are identified with keys

topics.name: Invertebrates and Fungi in the Ecosystem

Organisms are studied in their ecosystem

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Interactions: Competition, Symbiosis, Parasitism

Predator–prey builds on food chains

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Food Webs, Energy Flow and Trophic Levels

Energy enters by photosynthesis and leaves by respiration

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Carbon Cycle and Climate Change

topics.name: Biodiversity and Nature Conservation

evidence: Explains three levels of biodiversity with examples

Evaluates a local conservation measure and suggests one action pupils can take

Builds on nature protection from primary school

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Tolerance Curves and Ecological Potency

evidence: Reads optimum and tolerance range from a curve
Explains why the ecological optimum differs from the physiological one using competition
Explains why stenök species are good indicators
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that a plant grows best in moist soil in the lab but is found in dry places in nature, can they explain the difference?

Competition shifts the ecological optimum

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Ecological Niche and Competitive Exclusion

Distinguishes fundamental and realised niche

Competition determines the realised niche

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Predator–Prey Dynamics

Explains why real populations rarely oscillate as neatly as the model

The Lotka–Volterra model is judged against data

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Population Growth and Life Strategies

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: The Nitrogen Cycle

Decomposers return nitrogen to the soil

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Ecological Effects of Global Warming

Range shifts follow from tolerance limits

topics.subject: Biologie
topics.name: Ecosystem Management and Sustainable Use

Explains with a population curve why fishing above the sustainable yield collapses a stock

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Identifying Substances by Their Properties

topics.subject: Chemie

topics.name: The Periodic Table as a Tool

topics.name: Element Families: Alkali Metals, Halogens, Noble Gases

Ion charges are read from the group
