topics.name: Conservation of Mass
topics.nameDe: Gesetz von der Erhaltung der Masse
topics.description: Pupils show in closed-system experiments that the total mass stays the same in a reaction, explain apparent mass gains (burning steel wool) or losses (burning a candle) and justify the law with atoms being rearranged.
evidence: Explains why burnt steel wool is heavier than before
Plans an experiment in a closed system that shows conservation of mass
Explains the law with atom models
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a candle getting lighter as it burns, can they explain where the mass has gone?

prerequisites.reason: Combustion experiments show apparent mass changes

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Water: Analysis and Synthesis
topics.nameDe: Wasser als Verbindung: Analyse und Synthese
topics.description: Pupils show that water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen (electrolysis) and formed from them (oxyhydrogen test), use this as an example of the reversibility of reactions and discuss hydrogen as an energy carrier.
evidence: Describes the decomposition of water and the volume ratio of the gases
Explains the synthesis of water as the reverse reaction with the energy involved
Describes one advantage and one problem of hydrogen as a fuel
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that hydrogen cars only emit water, can they explain where the energy comes from and where it was put in?

prerequisites.reason: Water is decomposed into its elements
Hydrogen and oxygen are identified by tests

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations
topics.description: Pupils translate word equations into formula equations, balance them with coefficients so that atom numbers are conserved, and distinguish the meaning of index and coefficient.
evidence: Balances equations such as the combustion of methane or the formation of iron oxide
Explains the difference between 2 H₂O and H₂O₂
Translates a formula equation into a sentence on substance and particle level
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} writes "H₂ + O₂ → H₂O", can they explain what is wrong and fix it?

prerequisites.reason: Formulas stand for atoms and their ratios
Balancing expresses conservation of atoms

topics.laenderNotes: Formula equations come in Kl. 8 in most plans; NRW uses mostly word equations in the first stage.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Amount of Substance and Molar Mass
topics.description: Pupils explain the mole as a counting unit (Avogadro constant), calculate molar masses from the periodic table, convert between mass, amount and number of particles, and use the molar volume of gases.
evidence: Calculates the molar mass of a compound
Converts a mass into an amount of substance and number of particles
Explains why one mole of different substances has different masses
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked how many water molecules are in a 18 g sip of water, can they work it out?

prerequisites.reason: Formulas give the particle ratios
Large numbers are written as powers

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: scientific notation with powers of ten
externalPrerequisites.reason: The Avogadro constant is written as 6.022·10²³

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Kl. 9 (NTG Kl. 8), BW 8–10, NRW second stage (IF9), Berlin/Brandenburg 7/8 or 9/10.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Stoichiometric Calculations
topics.description: Pupils calculate masses and volumes of reactants and products from a balanced equation via amount ratios, apply the law of constant proportions and derive empirical formulas from measured masses.
evidence: Calculates the mass of product from a given mass of reactant
Derives an empirical formula from mass data of a synthesis
Explains why the mass ratio of the elements in a compound is fixed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to make 10 g of copper sulfide, can they calculate how much copper and sulfur to weigh out?

prerequisites.reason: Calculations go via amounts of substance
Proportional reasoning is the core of the calculation

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Concentration of Solutions
topics.description: Pupils use mass fraction, mass concentration and amount concentration (c = n/V), prepare solutions of given concentration and calculate dilutions.
evidence: Calculates the amount concentration of a solution from mass and volume
Prepares 100 mL of a 0.1 mol/L sodium chloride solution step by step
Calculates the concentration after a tenfold dilution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make a weaker solution from a stock bottle, can they calculate how much to take and how much water to add?

prerequisites.reason: Amount concentration uses the mole
Mass fractions are percentages
Volumes are converted between mL and L

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
topics.description: Pupils explain that substances store chemical energy, that reactions release (exothermic) or absorb (endothermic) energy as heat or light, and show the energy change in a simple energy diagram.
evidence: Classifies given reactions as exothermic or endothermic from observations
Draws an energy diagram for an exothermic and an endothermic reaction
Names different forms into which chemical energy is converted
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a hand warmer, can they explain where the heat comes from in terms of chemical energy?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on energy forms and conversion chains
Energy change is a sign of a reaction

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Activation Energy
topics.description: Pupils explain why many exothermic reactions must first be started by supplying energy (match, spark), show activation energy as a hill in the energy diagram and connect it to ignition temperature.
evidence: Adds the activation energy to an energy diagram
Explains why a sparkler needs a flame to start but then keeps burning
Distinguishes activation energy from the energy needed by an endothermic reaction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders why a gas stove does not ignite by itself, can they explain it with an energy diagram?

prerequisites.reason: Activation energy is added to the energy diagram
Ignition temperature was met with combustion

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Catalysts
topics.description: Pupils explain that a catalyst speeds up a reaction by offering a path with lower activation energy without being used up, and give examples from industry (ammonia synthesis), cars (Abgaskatalysator) and living things (enzymes).
evidence: Shows the effect of a catalyst in an energy diagram
Demonstrates with hydrogen peroxide and manganese dioxide that the catalyst is not used up
Explains how a car catalytic converter reduces pollutants
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that a catalyst "provides the energy" for a reaction, can they correct the statement?

prerequisites.reason: Catalysts lower the activation energy
Industrial examples are written as equations

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Reaction Enthalpy and the First Law
topics.description: Pupils describe a reaction as a system exchanging energy with its surroundings, apply the first law of thermodynamics, and use molar reaction enthalpies and standard enthalpies of formation to calculate ΔH.
evidence: Distinguishes open, closed and isolated systems
Calculates ΔH of a reaction from standard enthalpies of formation
Interprets the sign of ΔH and draws the enthalpy diagram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares the heat released by burning methane and hydrogen, can they calculate and compare the reaction enthalpies per mole and per gram?

prerequisites.reason: Quantifies exothermic and endothermic reactions
Enthalpies are given per mole

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Calorimetry
topics.description: Pupils determine reaction enthalpies (e.g. neutralisation, dissolving) with a simple calorimeter using Q = m·c·ΔT, and discuss sources of error such as heat loss.
evidence: Carries out a calorimetric measurement and calculates the molar enthalpy
Names two sources of error and their effect on the result
Compares the measured value with the literature value
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} mixes hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution in a coffee-cup calorimeter, can they calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation from the temperature rise?

prerequisites.reason: Calorimetry measures enthalpy changes
Neutralisation is the standard experiment

externalPrerequisites.subject: Physik
externalPrerequisites.concept: specific heat capacity and Q = m·c·ΔT
externalPrerequisites.reason: Calorimetry uses the heat equation

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Hess's Law
topics.description: Pupils apply Hess's law to calculate enthalpies of reactions that cannot be measured directly by combining known reaction steps in enthalpy cycles.
evidence: Calculates the enthalpy of formation of carbon monoxide from combustion enthalpies
Draws an enthalpy cycle and explains why the path does not matter
Explains the connection to the conservation of energy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} cannot burn carbon to carbon monoxide only, can they still calculate the enthalpy of that reaction from other data?

prerequisites.reason: Hess's law combines reaction enthalpies

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Entropy and Gibbs Free Energy
topics.description: Pupils explain entropy as a measure of the number of possible arrangements, the second law, and use ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS to predict whether a reaction can run spontaneously and how this depends on temperature.
evidence: Predicts the sign of ΔS for given reactions
Calculates ΔG and decides whether a reaction is spontaneous at a given temperature
Explains why an endothermic reaction can still run by itself
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that ice melts at room temperature although melting takes in heat, can they explain it with entropy?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on enthalpy calculations
Spontaneity is linked to equilibrium position

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Reaction Rate
topics.description: Pupils define reaction rate as change in concentration per time, determine average and instantaneous rates from measured curves (gas volume, mass loss, colour change) and explain why the rate decreases during a reaction.
evidence: Measures gas volume over time for marble and hydrochloric acid and plots the curve
Calculates an average rate from two points and estimates an instantaneous rate from a tangent
Explains why the curve flattens as the reaction proceeds
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records the gas produced by an effervescent tablet every 10 seconds, can they say when the reaction was fastest and why?

prerequisites.reason: Rates are changes in concentration
Rates depend on how many particles overcome the barrier

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: average and instantaneous rate of change (difference quotient, tangent slope)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Rates are read as slopes of concentration–time curves

topics.laenderNotes: NRW G9 Einführungsphase (Kl. 11); in G8 Länder Kl. 10/11.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Factors Affecting Rate: The Collision Model
topics.description: Pupils explain with the collision model how concentration, temperature (RGT rule), surface area and catalysts change the rate, and design experiments that vary one factor at a time.
evidence: Explains each factor with the frequency and energy of effective collisions
Plans an experiment on the effect of temperature with controlled variables
Applies the RGT rule to estimate a rate at a different temperature
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wonders why food keeps longer in the fridge, can they explain it with the collision model?

prerequisites.reason: Factors are compared by their effect on the rate
Catalysis is one factor
Collisions are particle motion

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium
topics.description: Pupils explain reversible reactions that reach equilibrium when forward and reverse rates are equal, distinguish the static appearance on the substance level from the dynamic state on the particle level, and use model experiments (Stechheber) to illustrate it.
evidence: Explains with rate curves when equilibrium is reached
Explains why equilibrium does not mean equal concentrations
Interprets a model experiment and names its limits
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an esterification flask where nothing seems to change, can they explain what is still happening at particle level?

prerequisites.reason: Reversibility of reactions was introduced in Sek I
Equilibrium means equal forward and reverse rates

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Le Chatelier's Principle
topics.description: Pupils predict how an equilibrium shifts when concentration, pressure or temperature change (Prinzip vom kleinsten Zwang) and check predictions with experiments such as the NO₂/N₂O₄ or the iron thiocyanate equilibrium.
evidence: Predicts the shift for changes in concentration, pressure and temperature
Explains a colour change in the NO₂/N₂O₄ system on heating or cooling
Explains why a catalyst does not shift the equilibrium
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} warms a sealed tube of brown NO₂ gas and it gets darker, can they explain which direction is endothermic?

prerequisites.reason: The principle describes how equilibria respond

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: The Law of Mass Action
topics.description: Pupils write the equilibrium constant Kc for a reaction, calculate Kc and equilibrium concentrations from data, and interpret the size of Kc as the position of equilibrium.
evidence: Writes the Kc expression for a given equation
Calculates Kc from equilibrium concentrations and an equilibrium concentration from Kc
Interprets Kc ≫ 1 and Kc ≪ 1
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given the starting amounts of acid and alcohol in an esterification, can they calculate how much ester is present at equilibrium?

prerequisites.reason: Kc describes the equilibrium state
Kc is built from concentrations

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: solving equations including quadratic equations
externalPrerequisites.reason: Equilibrium concentrations are found by solving equations

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Equilibrium in Industry: the Haber–Bosch Process
topics.description: Pupils explain the conditions of ammonia synthesis as a compromise between equilibrium yield and rate (pressure, temperature, catalyst, removing ammonia) and evaluate its importance for fertiliser and its energy cost.
evidence: Justifies the chosen pressure and temperature with Le Chatelier and kinetics
Explains the role of the catalyst and of removing ammonia continuously
Evaluates the process with respect to food security and energy use
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that the process runs at about 450 °C although lower temperatures give more ammonia, can they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Conditions are chosen with Le Chatelier
Rate considerations limit low temperatures

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Solubility Equilibria
topics.description: Pupils describe the equilibrium between a solid salt and its dissolved ions with the solubility product, calculate solubilities and predict precipitation, including the common-ion effect.
evidence: Writes the solubility product expression for a sparingly soluble salt
Calculates the solubility from KL
Predicts whether a precipitate forms when two solutions are mixed
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} adds sodium chloride to a saturated silver chloride solution, can they predict and explain what happens?

prerequisites.reason: The solubility product is a law-of-mass-action constant
Builds on dissolving of salts

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Acidic and Alkaline Solutions
topics.description: Pupils investigate everyday acidic and alkaline solutions with indicators (red cabbage, universal indicator), describe their properties (conductivity, reaction with metals and lime, corrosive effect) and handle them safely.
evidence: Sorts household solutions into acidic, neutral and alkaline with an indicator
Describes the reactions of an acid with magnesium and with lime and identifies the gases
Gives safety measures for working with concentrated acids and alkalis
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} tests vinegar, soap solution and tap water with red cabbage juice, can they explain the colours?

prerequisites.reason: Acidity is one property of solutions
Acids and alkalis are hazardous substances
Hydrogen and CO₂ are identified by tests

topics.laenderNotes: NRW second stage (IF9), Bayern Kl. 10, BW 8–10, Berlin/Brandenburg 7/8 or 9/10.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: The pH Scale
topics.description: Pupils measure pH values with indicators and pH meters, use the 0–14 scale, and show by tenfold dilution that one pH step corresponds to a factor of ten in acidity.
evidence: Measures and compares the pH of several solutions
Shows by dilution of hydrochloric acid that the pH rises by one per tenfold dilution
Explains why "pH 3 is twice as acidic as pH 6" is wrong
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} dilutes lemon juice ten times, can they predict the change in pH?

prerequisites.reason: pH quantifies acidity
Steps of ten are powers of ten

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Oxonium and Hydroxide Ions
topics.description: Pupils explain that acidic solutions contain oxonium ions (H₃O⁺) and alkaline solutions hydroxide ions (OH⁻), how these form when hydrogen chloride or a metal oxide reacts with water, and why such solutions conduct electricity.
evidence: Writes the equation for the reaction of hydrogen chloride with water
Explains how sodium hydroxide or calcium oxide forms an alkaline solution
Explains the conductivity of acidic and alkaline solutions with ions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that dry hydrogen chloride does not conduct but its solution does, can they explain the difference?

prerequisites.reason: Explains the properties of acidic and alkaline solutions
Ions and ionic formulas are needed
HCl is a polar molecule that reacts with water dipoles

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Acids and Bases as Proton Donors and Acceptors
topics.description: Pupils define acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors, identify conjugate acid–base pairs, recognise water as an ampholyte and see acid–base reactions as donor–acceptor reactions.
evidence: Identifies acid, base and conjugate pairs in a given equation
Explains why water can act as acid and as base
Explains why ammonia is a base though it contains no hydroxide
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees ammonia gas turn indicator paper blue, can they explain with proton transfer why it is a base?

prerequisites.reason: Proton transfer explains oxonium ion formation

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Neutralisation and Salt Formation
topics.description: Pupils explain neutralisation as the reaction of oxonium and hydroxide ions to water, show that the remaining ions form a salt, observe the heat released and apply neutralisation to everyday cases (antacids, liming soils).
evidence: Writes the ionic equation of a neutralisation
Names the salt formed from a given acid and base
Explains how an antacid tablet relieves heartburn
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} mixes hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution until neutral and evaporates the water, can they explain what remains?

prerequisites.reason: Neutralisation is a proton transfer
The product salt is an ionic compound

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Acid–Base Titration with an Indicator
topics.description: Pupils carry out a titration with burette and indicator, read the volume at the colour change and calculate the unknown concentration with the stoichiometry of the neutralisation.
evidence: Carries out a titration accurately and reads the burette correctly
Calculates the concentration of an unknown acid from the titration volume
Names sources of error in a titration
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} titrates vinegar with sodium hydroxide solution, can they calculate its acetic acid content and compare it with the label?

prerequisites.reason: The end point is complete neutralisation
Concentration is calculated stoichiometrically

topics.laenderNotes: BW Kl. 8–10; NRW Grundkurs Q-phase; in the KMK Abitur standards titration with indicator end point is gA, titration curves eA.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Acid Strength: Ka and pKa
topics.description: Pupils apply the law of mass action to protolysis equilibria, define Ka/pKa and Kb/pKb, rank acids and bases by strength, and predict the direction of acid–base reactions from pKa values.
evidence: Writes the Ka expression and relates pKa to acid strength
Ranks given acids by strength using a pKa table
Predicts whether an acid–base reaction proceeds by comparing pKa values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares the pKa values of acetic acid and hydrochloric acid, can they explain why the same concentration gives different pH values?

prerequisites.reason: Protolysis is proton transfer
Ka is a law-of-mass-action constant

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: pH Calculations for Strong Acids and Bases
topics.description: Pupils explain the autoprotolysis of water and Kw, define pH and pOH as negative logarithms and calculate pH values of solutions of strong acids and bases.
evidence: Calculates the pH of 0.01 mol/L hydrochloric acid and of 0.01 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution
Explains why pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C
Calculates the oxonium concentration from a given pH
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows the pH of a cleaning solution is 12, can they calculate the hydroxide concentration?

prerequisites.reason: Kw is an equilibrium constant like Ka
Builds on the pH scale from Sek I

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: logarithms to base 10
externalPrerequisites.reason: pH is a negative decimal logarithm

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: pH of Weak Acids and Bases
topics.description: Pupils calculate pH values of weak acids and bases with the Ka/Kb relation and the usual approximation, and check when the approximation is valid.
evidence: Calculates the pH of 0.1 mol/L acetic acid
Calculates the pH of an ammonia solution via Kb
Explains when the approximation for weak acids fails
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures pH 2.9 for 0.1 mol/L acetic acid, can they show by calculation that this fits its Ka value?

prerequisites.reason: Extends pH calculation to incomplete protolysis

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Buffer Solutions
topics.description: Pupils explain how a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base resists pH changes, calculate buffer pH with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, and describe the carbonate buffer of blood.
evidence: Explains with equations how a buffer reacts to added acid and added base
Calculates the pH of an acetate buffer
Explains the role of the hydrogen carbonate buffer in blood
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} adds a few drops of hydrochloric acid to water and to a buffer, can they predict and explain the different pH changes?

prerequisites.reason: Buffers are built from weak acids
Buffer action is an equilibrium shift

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Titration Curves
topics.description: Pupils record and interpret pH titration curves of strong and weak acids, locate the equivalence point and half-equivalence point (pH = pKa), and choose a suitable indicator.
evidence: Records a titration curve with a pH meter and marks the equivalence point
Reads the pKa of a weak acid from the half-equivalence point
Explains why phenolphthalein suits the titration of acetic acid but methyl orange does not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares the titration curves of hydrochloric acid and acetic acid, can they explain why the equivalence points lie at different pH values?

prerequisites.reason: Extends end-point titration to pH curves
The flat region of the curve is a buffer region

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Metal Extraction by Oxygen Transfer
topics.description: Pupils explain the reduction of metal oxides by carbon or a more reactive metal as oxygen transfer (oxidation and reduction as one redox reaction), order metals as noble or base by their affinity for oxygen, and describe the blast furnace and the thermite reaction.
evidence: Identifies oxidation, reduction, oxidising agent and reducing agent in an oxygen-transfer reaction
Predicts whether a metal can reduce a given metal oxide from a reactivity series
Describes the main reactions in a blast furnace
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heats copper oxide with carbon, can they explain what happens to each substance and why iron oxide needs much more energy?

prerequisites.reason: Oxidation was introduced as reaction with oxygen
Redox reactions are written as equations

topics.laenderNotes: NRW first stage (IF4), Berlin/Brandenburg 7/8; BW and Bayern go straight to the electron-transfer view.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Redox as Electron Transfer
topics.description: Pupils extend oxidation and reduction to electron release and uptake, write half-equations for reactions of metals with metal-ion solutions (iron in copper sulfate), and order metals and their ions in a redox series.
evidence: Writes oxidation, reduction and overall equations for a metal–metal-ion reaction
Orders three metals by experimental results into a redox series
Explains the donor–acceptor principle for electron transfer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} dips an iron nail into copper sulfate solution and it turns red-brown, can they explain the reaction with electron transfer?

prerequisites.reason: Generalises oxygen transfer to electron transfer
Metal ions form by electron loss

osMatches.note: os displacement reactions without electron transfer

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Galvanic Cells and Batteries
topics.description: Pupils explain how a galvanic cell (Daniell cell) separates oxidation and reduction so that electrons flow through a wire, distinguish batteries, rechargeable accumulators and fuel cells, and judge which is suitable for a use.
evidence: Labels anode, cathode, electron flow and salt bridge in a Daniell cell
Explains the difference between a battery and an accumulator
Chooses a suitable power source for a use with reasons
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a lemon battery with a zinc and a copper plate, can they explain where the electrons come from?

prerequisites.reason: The cell uses a redox reaction
Current needs a closed circuit

externalPrerequisites.subject: Physik
externalPrerequisites.concept: electric current and voltage in a circuit
externalPrerequisites.reason: Cell voltage and current are measured physically

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Electrolysis
topics.description: Pupils carry out electrolysis of a salt solution (zinc iodide, copper chloride), explain the reactions at the electrodes and see electrolysis as the reverse of a galvanic cell that stores electrical energy as chemical energy.
evidence: Identifies the products at both electrodes of a zinc iodide electrolysis
Writes the electrode reactions
Explains why charging an accumulator is an electrolysis
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees zinc forming at one electrode and iodine at the other, can they explain which electrode is which and why?

prerequisites.reason: Electrolysis is the reverse process
Water decomposition was a first electrolysis

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Oxidation Numbers and Redox Equations
topics.description: Pupils assign oxidation numbers with rules, identify oxidation and reduction in complex and organic reactions, and balance redox equations with half-equations in acidic and alkaline solution.
evidence: Assigns oxidation numbers to all atoms in given molecules and ions
Balances the reaction of permanganate with iron(II) ions in acidic solution
Identifies the oxidised atom when ethanol is oxidised
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a breathalyser reaction with dichromate, can they show with oxidation numbers what is oxidised and what reduced?

prerequisites.reason: Oxidation numbers formalise electron transfer
Oxidation numbers assign shared electrons by electronegativity

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Standard Potentials and the Electrochemical Series
topics.description: Pupils explain half-cells and the standard hydrogen electrode, read the electrochemical series and predict whether a redox reaction occurs spontaneously from standard potentials.
evidence: Explains how standard potentials are measured against the hydrogen electrode
Predicts the reaction between two redox pairs from their potentials
Explains why base metals dissolve in acids and noble metals do not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks up the standard potentials of zinc and copper, can they predict which metal dissolves in a solution of the other's ions?

prerequisites.reason: Redox pairs are written as half-equations
Half-cells combine to galvanic cells

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Calculating Cell Voltage
topics.description: Pupils build galvanic cells from half-cells, calculate the cell voltage as the difference of standard potentials (ΔE = E(Kathode) − E(Anode)) and compare calculated and measured values.
evidence: Calculates the cell voltage of a Daniell cell and of a silver–copper cell
Identifies anode and cathode from the potentials
Explains why the measured voltage of a cell drops when current flows
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given four half-cells, can they choose the pair with the highest voltage and calculate it?

prerequisites.reason: Cell voltage is calculated from standard potentials

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Batteries, Accumulators and Fuel Cells
topics.description: Pupils explain the electrode reactions of a lead-acid battery, a lithium-ion battery and a hydrogen fuel cell, and evaluate them for mobility and energy storage (capacity, raw materials, recycling).
evidence: Writes the discharge reactions of a lead-acid battery
Explains how a lithium-ion battery works during charging and discharging
Evaluates the fuel cell versus the battery for cars with several criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a battery electric car with a hydrogen car, can they explain the chemistry of both and weigh their pros and cons?

prerequisites.reason: Power sources are galvanic cells
Charging is electrolysis

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Electrolysis and Decomposition Voltage
topics.description: Pupils determine the decomposition voltage of an electrolysis, predict electrode products from potentials, and describe industrial electrolyses such as chlor-alkali electrolysis and water electrolysis for green hydrogen.
evidence: Determines the decomposition voltage from a current–voltage curve
Predicts the products of the electrolysis of a sodium chloride solution
Evaluates green hydrogen from water electrolysis as an energy carrier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} electrolyses salt water, can they explain why chlorine and hydrogen form rather than sodium?

prerequisites.reason: Deepens the Sek I view of electrolysis
Products are predicted from potentials

topics.laenderNotes: Faraday's laws and overpotential are eA only (KMK 2020).

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Corrosion and Corrosion Protection
topics.description: Pupils explain rusting as oxygen and acid corrosion with local cells, and how coatings, galvanising and sacrificial anodes protect metals.
evidence: Writes the reactions of iron rusting in moist air
Explains why a scratched galvanised sheet still does not rust while a scratched tin can does
Explains how a sacrificial anode protects a ship
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees zinc blocks on a ship's hull, can they explain why they are there and why they must be replaced?

prerequisites.reason: Protection depends on standard potentials

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: The Nernst Equation and Concentration Cells
topics.description: Pupils use the Nernst equation to calculate electrode potentials at non-standard concentrations, explain concentration cells and the potentiometric pH measurement.
evidence: Calculates the potential of a copper half-cell at 0.01 mol/L
Calculates the voltage of a concentration cell
Explains how a pH electrode uses the concentration dependence of a potential
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a cell from two copper half-cells with different concentrations, can they predict the voltage and which side is the anode?

prerequisites.reason: Extends standard potentials to any concentration
Logarithmic concentration terms like pH

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis
topics.description: Pupils relate charge, current and time to the amount of substance deposited in electrolysis (n = I·t / (z·F)), and apply this to electroplating and hydrogen production.
evidence: Calculates the mass of copper deposited by a given current and time
Calculates the time needed to produce a given volume of hydrogen
Explains why the actual yield is often lower than calculated
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to copper-plate a key with 0.5 g of copper, can they calculate how long to run a 1 A current?

prerequisites.reason: Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis
Results are amounts of substance

externalPrerequisites.subject: Physik
externalPrerequisites.concept: electric charge as current times time (Q = I·t)
externalPrerequisites.reason: The calculation starts from transported charge

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Alkanes and the Homologous Series
topics.description: Pupils describe alkanes from methane to decane with molecular and structural formulas (CnH2n+2), explain the trends in boiling point and viscosity within the homologous series with van der Waals forces, and describe their combustion.
evidence: Writes molecular and structural formulas of the first ten alkanes
Explains the rise in boiling point with chain length
Writes the equation for the complete combustion of propane
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares camping gas (propane/butane) and candle wax, can they explain why one is a gas and the other a solid at room temperature?

prerequisites.reason: Alkanes are built from covalent C–C and C–H bonds
Boiling-point trends come from van der Waals forces

topics.laenderNotes: Organic chemistry starts in Kl. 9/10 almost everywhere (NRW IF10, Berlin/Brandenburg 9/10, Bayern Kl. 10, BW 8–10).

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Naming Organic Compounds and Isomers
topics.description: Pupils name branched alkanes and simple compounds of other classes by IUPAC rules, draw structures from names, and explain constitutional isomers with their different properties.
evidence: Names a branched alkane correctly and draws the structure for a given name
Draws all isomers of pentane and names them
Explains why isomers have different boiling points
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the name 2,2-dimethylpropane, can they draw the molecule and explain why it boils lower than pentane?

prerequisites.reason: Nomenclature starts from the alkane names

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Alcohols: Ethanol and the Alkanols
topics.description: Pupils describe the hydroxy group as the functional group of alcohols, explain solubility and boiling point of alkanols from the polar OH group and the non-polar chain, describe ethanol production by fermentation and evaluate uses and health risks of ethanol.
evidence: Explains why ethanol mixes with water but decanol does not
Explains the higher boiling point of ethanol compared with propane
Describes risks of alcohol consumption and uses of ethanol as solvent and disinfectant
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that ethanol dissolves both in water and in petrol, can they explain this from the structure of the molecule?

prerequisites.reason: Alkanols are alkanes with an OH group
Properties follow from hydrogen bonds
Ethanol is made by alcoholic fermentation

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Oxidation Series: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids
topics.nameDe: Oxidationsreihe der Alkanole: Alkanale, Alkanone, Alkansäuren
topics.description: Pupils explain how primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and carboxylic acids and secondary alcohols to ketones, use oxidation numbers to follow the C atom, and identify carbonyl compounds with tests (Fehling, Tollens, Schiff).
evidence: Predicts the oxidation products of a primary, secondary and tertiary alcohol
Assigns oxidation numbers to the functional carbon atom along the series
Uses the Fehling or Tollens test to distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} oxidises ethanol and propan-2-ol, can they predict which product gives a positive Fehling test and why?

prerequisites.reason: The series starts from alcohols
Oxidation is tracked with oxidation numbers

topics.laenderNotes: NRW G9 Einführungsphase; Bayern, BW and Berlin/Brandenburg already in Kl. 10 (Sek I).

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Carboxylic Acids
topics.description: Pupils describe the carboxy group, explain why carboxylic acids are weak acids, compare properties (boiling point, solubility, acidity) along the homologous series and name everyday uses (vinegar, citric acid, fatty acids).
evidence: Explains the acidity of acetic acid with proton release from the carboxy group
Compares boiling points of acetic acid, ethanol and ethanal and explains the order
Names two everyday carboxylic acids and their uses
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} descales a kettle with citric acid, can they explain which part of the molecule does the work?

prerequisites.reason: Carboxylic acids are the end of the oxidation series
Acidity is proton donation

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Ester Synthesis and Hydrolysis
topics.description: Pupils carry out the acid-catalysed condensation of an alcohol and a carboxylic acid to an ester, explain the reaction as an equilibrium that can be shifted, and relate esters to fragrances, fats and polyesters.
evidence: Writes the equation for the formation of ethyl ethanoate
Explains how removing water or using excess alcohol increases the ester yield
Names an ester from its structure and the acid and alcohol it comes from
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} makes a fruity smelling ester in the lab, can they explain why adding sulfuric acid and excess alcohol helps?

prerequisites.reason: Esters form from carboxylic acids
The alcohol is the second reactant of esterification
The yield is improved by shifting the equilibrium

topics.laenderNotes: The mechanism of ester synthesis is eA only (KMK 2020).

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Alkenes and Multiple Bonds
topics.description: Pupils describe alkenes and alkynes with C=C and C≡C bonds, their geometry, cis–trans isomerism and higher reactivity, and detect double bonds with bromine water.
evidence: Draws ethene and ethyne with correct bond angles
Draws cis and trans isomers of but-2-ene and explains why they cannot interconvert
Uses the bromine water test to distinguish an alkene from an alkane
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shakes hexene and hexane with bromine water, can they predict which one decolourises it and why?

prerequisites.reason: Alkenes are named and drawn like alkanes
Geometry follows from electron pairs

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Electrophilic Addition
topics.description: Pupils describe the mechanism of electrophilic addition of bromine to an alkene (polarisation, π-complex, bromonium ion, nucleophilic attack) with curved arrows and use it to explain experimental evidence.
evidence: Writes the mechanism with curved arrows and intermediates
Explains why adding bromine in salt water also gives a bromo-chloro product
Distinguishes electrophile and nucleophile
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets two products when bromine adds to ethene in sodium chloride solution, can they explain this with the mechanism?

prerequisites.reason: Addition happens at the double bond
Polarisation drives the mechanism

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Radical Substitution
topics.description: Pupils describe the halogenation of alkanes as a radical chain reaction (start, chain propagation, termination), explain the role of light and the product mixture.
evidence: Writes the start, propagation and termination steps
Explains why the reaction needs light and runs as a chain
Explains why several halogenated products form
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees methane and chlorine react only in light, can they explain what light does and why the reaction goes on after the light is off?

prerequisites.reason: Alkanes react by substitution
Homolytic bond splitting creates radicals

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Nucleophilic Substitution (SN1 and SN2)
topics.description: Pupils describe SN1 and SN2 mechanisms for haloalkanes, explain how structure, solvent and nucleophile decide which mechanism runs, and relate rate laws to the mechanisms.
evidence: Writes SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with curved arrows
Predicts the mechanism for a primary and a tertiary haloalkane
Explains how rate data distinguish the two mechanisms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that the rate of a substitution does not depend on the nucleophile concentration, can they explain which mechanism is at work?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on curved-arrow mechanisms
Mechanisms are linked to reaction rates

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Aromatic Compounds and Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
topics.description: Pupils explain the structure of benzene with delocalised electrons (mesomerism, resonance energy), why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition, and the mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution (e.g. bromination).
evidence: Explains the Kekulé problem and the mesomeric structure of benzene
Explains with resonance energy why benzene reacts by substitution
Writes the mechanism of the bromination of benzene with a catalyst
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that benzene does not decolourise bromine water, can they explain why although it has double bonds in its formula?

prerequisites.reason: Substitution is contrasted with addition
Resonance energy is derived from enthalpy data

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Chirality and Optical Activity
topics.description: Pupils identify stereocentres, draw enantiomers in Fischer projection, explain optical activity measured with a polarimeter and the biological importance of chirality (amino acids, drugs).
evidence: Marks the stereocentre and draws both enantiomers of lactic acid
Explains how a polarimeter distinguishes enantiomers
Explains why one enantiomer of a drug can be harmful
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns about the thalidomide (Contergan) case, can they explain the role of chirality?

prerequisites.reason: Chirality is a form of isomerism
Tetrahedral carbon makes mirror images possible

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Plastics: Macromolecules in Everyday Life
topics.description: Pupils explain plastics as macromolecules built from many monomers, relate properties (flexibility, heat behaviour) to chain structure, and justify the choice of plastics for everyday products.
evidence: Explains the idea of a macromolecule with a chain model
Explains why many plastics soften when heated
Justifies the use of a plastic for a product from its properties
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a plastic bag and a light switch, can they explain why one melts easily and the other does not?

prerequisites.reason: Plastics are long carbon chains
Properties depend on forces between chains

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Polymer Synthesis: Polymerisation and Polycondensation
topics.description: Pupils explain how monomers with double bonds form polymers by polymerisation (polyethylene, PVC) and how bifunctional monomers form polyesters and polyamides by polycondensation, and derive monomers from a polymer structure.
evidence: Writes the formation of polyethylene and identifies the repeating unit
Explains the synthesis of a polyester or nylon by polycondensation
Derives the monomers from a given polymer section
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the structure of PET in a drinks bottle, can they identify the two monomers it was made from?

prerequisites.reason: Deepens Sek I macromolecules
Polymerisation opens double bonds
Polyesters are formed like esters

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Plastic Classes, Properties and Recycling
topics.description: Pupils explain thermoplastics, thermosets and elastomers from chain structure and cross-linking, and evaluate mechanical, chemical (feedstock) and energy recovery of plastic waste in terms of ecology and economy.
evidence: Assigns thermoplastics, thermosets and elastomers to their structure and behaviour on heating
Compares mechanical, feedstock and energy recycling
Evaluates a plastic product over its life cycle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sorts packaging into the yellow bin, can they explain what happens next and why not all plastics can be melted down again?

prerequisites.reason: Structure follows from the synthesis
Recycling and resources were met in Sek I

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Mechanism of Radical Polymerisation
topics.description: Pupils describe the start, growth and termination steps of radical polymerisation and explain how reaction conditions influence chain length and branching.
evidence: Writes the mechanism of radical polymerisation of ethene
Explains how branching occurs and how it affects density (LDPE vs HDPE)
Explains how an initiator concentration changes chain length
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares LDPE and HDPE, can they explain the difference in properties from the polymerisation mechanism?

prerequisites.reason: Mechanism of a known synthesis
Radical chain steps were met with substitution

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Fats and Oils
topics.description: Pupils describe fats as triglycerides (glycerol esters of fatty acids), explain how saturated and unsaturated fatty acids affect melting point, describe saponification and how soaps and surfactants clean.
evidence: Draws the structure of a triglyceride and names its building blocks
Explains why olive oil is liquid and butter is solid
Explains with a micelle model how soap removes grease
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads "rich in unsaturated fatty acids" on a margarine tub, can they explain what this means for the structure and melting behaviour?

prerequisites.reason: Fats are esters
Unsaturated fatty acids contain double bonds
Fats were met as nutrients in biology

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Amines, Amino Acids and the Peptide Bond
topics.description: Pupils describe the amino group and its basic character, the zwitterion structure of amino acids, and the formation of peptides by condensation, linking this to protein structure in biology.
evidence: Explains the basic reaction of the amino group with water
Draws an amino acid as a zwitterion and explains its high melting point
Writes the formation of a dipeptide and marks the peptide bond
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that amino acids are solids that dissolve in water, can they explain this with the zwitterion structure?

prerequisites.reason: Amino acids carry a carboxy group
The zwitterion forms by internal proton transfer
Protein structure was introduced in biology

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Carbohydrates
topics.description: Pupils describe glucose in chain and ring form, the glycosidic bond in disaccharides, and the structures of starch and cellulose, and explain why humans can digest one but not the other.
evidence: Draws glucose in chain and ring form and marks the functional groups
Explains the formation of maltose from two glucose units
Explains the different properties of starch and cellulose from their structure
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that cows can live on grass but people cannot, can they explain the chemical difference between starch and cellulose?

prerequisites.reason: Glucose contains carbonyl and hydroxy groups
Carbohydrates were met as nutrients

topics.laenderNotes: eA in KMK 2020 as a second natural-product class; Bayern Chemie 11 (Lebensmittelchemie) treats it for all pupils.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Tests for Gases and Water
topics.description: Pupils carry out and interpret standard tests: glowing splint (oxygen), oxyhydrogen test (hydrogen), limewater (carbon dioxide) and copper sulfate or Watesmo paper (water).
evidence: Carries out the four tests safely and describes a positive result
Chooses the right test to identify an unknown gas
Uses tests to show which products form when a candle burns
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} collects the gas from a reaction of magnesium with acid, can they prove which gas it is?

prerequisites.reason: The tested gases are components of air and combustion products
Hydrogen tests need safety precautions

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Tests for Ions: Precipitation and Flame Tests
topics.description: Pupils identify ions with precipitation reactions (chloride with silver nitrate, sulfate with barium chloride, carbonate with acid and limewater) and metal ions by flame colours, and analyse an unknown salt or mineral water.
evidence: Detects chloride and sulfate ions with precipitation tests
Identifies lithium, sodium and potassium by flame colour
Plans an analysis to identify an unknown salt and interprets the results
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads the label of a mineral water, can they test whether it really contains chloride and sulfate?

prerequisites.reason: Salts are made of ions that can be detected
Flame colours were seen with alkali metals

topics.laenderNotes: Many Länder introduce ion tests with salts in Sek I; NRW places them in the Oberstufe (Grundkurs), the KMK Abitur standards list them as gA.

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Chromatography
topics.description: Pupils explain chromatography by the distribution between stationary and mobile phase, calculate Rf values in thin-layer chromatography, choose solvents by polarity and interpret gas chromatograms.
evidence: Carries out a thin-layer chromatography and calculates Rf values
Explains the separation with polarity of the phases and the substances
Identifies a substance in a gas chromatogram from its retention time
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to find out whether a food dye contains a banned colourant, can they plan and interpret a chromatographic test?

prerequisites.reason: Deepens paper chromatography from Kl. 7
Separation depends on intermolecular forces

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Instrumental Analysis: Conductometry and Photometry
topics.description: Pupils use conductometric titration (conductivity against volume) and photometry (Lambert–Beer law, calibration line) to determine concentrations, and compare them with indicator methods.
evidence: Interprets a conductometric titration curve with the ions present in each section
Determines a concentration from a photometric calibration line
Explains when an instrumental method is better than an indicator
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to measure the concentration of a coloured solution without titrating, can they explain how a photometer and a calibration line help?

prerequisites.reason: Instrumental methods replace the indicator
Conductivity depends on ions in solution

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: linear functions and reading values from a line of best fit
externalPrerequisites.reason: Calibration lines are linear functions

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Metals as Resources and Recycling
topics.description: Pupils describe how metals are extracted from ores, why many metals (copper, aluminium, rare elements in phones) are scarce and energy-intensive to produce, and evaluate recycling and their own consumption.
evidence: Explains why recycling aluminium saves most of the energy needed for new aluminium
Names metals in a smartphone and where they come from
Suggests and evaluates a measure to save metal resources
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has an old phone in a drawer, can they explain why it is worth recycling and what happens to the metals?

prerequisites.reason: Metals are extracted by reducing ores
Builds on waste separation and recycling

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Fossil and Renewable Fuels
topics.description: Pupils describe crude oil refining by fractional distillation, compare the energy and CO₂ released by burning fuels (coal, natural gas, petrol, biofuels, hydrogen) and discuss their use from ecological, economic and ethical viewpoints.
evidence: Explains fractional distillation of crude oil with boiling ranges
Compares fuels by energy released and CO₂ produced per kilojoule
Discusses biofuels with at least one ecological and one ethical argument
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares a petrol car and a car running on biofuel, can they explain why biofuel is not automatically climate-neutral?

prerequisites.reason: Fuels are mostly hydrocarbons
Refining is distillation
Renewable and finite sources were introduced in primary school

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Greenhouse Gases and the Carbon Cycle
topics.description: Pupils explain which molecules act as greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour) and why, trace the sources of the rise in CO₂, describe the carbon cycle as a system of chemical reactions and evaluate ways to cut emissions.
evidence: Names the main greenhouse gases and their sources
Describes the carbon cycle with reaction equations for photosynthesis, respiration and combustion
Evaluates two measures to reduce CO₂ emissions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that methane is a stronger greenhouse gas than CO₂, can they explain where it comes from and why it still gets less attention?

prerequisites.reason: Burning fuels is the main CO₂ source
The carbon cycle was met in biology
CO₂ is a trace gas of the air

externalPrerequisites.subject: Erdkunde
externalPrerequisites.concept: the greenhouse effect and climate change
externalPrerequisites.reason: Geography explains the climate system

topics.subject: Chemie
topics.name: Nanomaterials
topics.description: Pupils explain why materials behave differently at the nanoscale (large surface-to-volume ratio, lotus effect, nanosilver, titanium dioxide in sun cream) and assess opportunities and risks of nanotechnology.
evidence: Calculates how the surface-to-volume ratio changes when a cube is divided
Explains the lotus effect with surface structure
Evaluates one nanoproduct with benefits and possible risks
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} buys a self-cleaning window coating, can they explain how the nanostructure makes dirt roll off?

prerequisites.reason: Surface effects depend on interactions
Nanomaterials are modern materials like plastics

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning what each part of a cell does, how specialised cells form tissues such as those in a leaf, and how single-celled and multicellular organisms differ.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, welche Aufgabe die Zellbestandteile haben, wie spezialisierte Zellen Gewebe bilden (z. B. im Laubblatt) und wie sich Einzeller und Vielzeller unterscheiden.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying the cell at electron-microscope level: compartments, the membrane model, diffusion, osmosis and transport, protein structure, and stem cells including the ethical debate around them.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind untersucht die Zelle auf elektronenmikroskopischer Ebene: Kompartimente, Biomembran, Diffusion, Osmose und Stofftransport, Proteinstruktur sowie Stammzellen und die ethische Debatte darüber.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is comparing photosynthesis and cell respiration, testing them in experiments, and learning how enzymes speed up reactions such as digestion.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind vergleicht Fotosynthese und Zellatmung, überprüft sie in Experimenten und lernt, wie Enzyme Reaktionen wie die Verdauung beschleunigen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how yeast and lactic acid bacteria release energy without oxygen and how this is used for bread, yoghurt and in our muscles.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Hefe und Milchsäurebakterien ohne Sauerstoff Energie gewinnen und wie das beim Brotbacken, für Joghurt und in unseren Muskeln genutzt wird.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is working through metabolism in detail: enzyme kinetics, ATP, the light reactions and Calvin cycle of photosynthesis, and glycolysis to the respiratory chain; Leistungskurs students also study C4 plants.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erarbeitet den Stoffwechsel im Detail: Enzymkinetik, ATP, Licht- und Calvin-Zyklus der Fotosynthese sowie Glykolyse bis Atmungskette; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich C4-Pflanzen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning what nutrients are made of, how to test foods for them, and how enzymes break food down so it can pass into the blood.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, woraus Nährstoffe bestehen, wie man sie in Lebensmitteln nachweist und wie Enzyme die Nahrung zerlegen, damit sie ins Blut gelangt.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how bacteria and viruses cause disease, how the immune system defends the body, how vaccines work and why antibiotics must be used carefully.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Bakterien und Viren Krankheiten auslösen, wie das Immunsystem den Körper schützt, wie Impfungen wirken und warum Antibiotika sorgfältig eingesetzt werden müssen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how hormones control the menstrual cycle, how contraception and condoms work, how to protect against sexually transmitted infections, and to talk respectfully about sexual diversity and consent.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Hormone den Zyklus steuern, wie Verhütung und Kondome wirken, wie man sich vor sexuell übertragbaren Infektionen schützt und wie man respektvoll über sexuelle Vielfalt und Einvernehmlichkeit spricht.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to weigh different positions on abortion with facts about prenatal development and the legal situation in Germany.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, Positionen zum Schwangerschaftsabbruch mit Wissen über die vorgeburtliche Entwicklung und die Rechtslage in Deutschland abzuwägen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how senses, nerves and the brain work together, how the eye sees, how hormones such as insulin regulate the body, and what happens in the body under stress.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Sinne, Nerven und Gehirn zusammenarbeiten, wie das Auge sieht, wie Hormone wie Insulin den Körper regeln und was bei Stress im Körper passiert.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how drugs act at the synapses and why addiction develops.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Drogen an den Synapsen wirken und wie Sucht entsteht.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying how nerve cells create and pass on electrical signals, how synapses work and how drugs and toxins interfere with them; Leistungskurs students also study summation, sensory cells and learning.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind untersucht, wie Nervenzellen elektrische Signale erzeugen und weiterleiten, wie Synapsen funktionieren und wie Gifte und Drogen eingreifen; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Verrechnung, Sinneszellen und Lernen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning about chromosomes and DNA, mitosis and meiosis, Mendel's rules and family pedigrees, chromosome disorders such as trisomy 21, and the basics of genetic engineering.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt Chromosomen und DNA, Mitose und Meiose, die Mendelschen Regeln und Stammbäume, Chromosomenstörungen wie Trisomie 21 und die Grundlagen der Gentechnik kennen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying molecular genetics: DNA replication, transcription and translation, mutations, gene regulation and epigenetics, genetic testing and counselling; Leistungskurs students also study cancer, PCR and genetic engineering methods.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erarbeitet die Molekulargenetik: Replikation, Transkription und Translation, Mutationen, Genregulation und Epigenetik, Gentests und genetische Beratung; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Krebs, PCR und gentechnische Verfahren.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning Darwin's theory of natural selection, the evidence for evolution, how new species arise, how organisms are classified and how humans evolved.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt Darwins Selektionstheorie, Belege für die Evolution, die Entstehung neuer Arten, das natürliche System und die Evolution des Menschen kennen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying the modern theory of evolution: evolutionary factors, speciation, coevolution, molecular family trees and the adaptive value of behaviour; Leistungskurs students also study population genetics and human and cultural evolution.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erarbeitet die Synthetische Evolutionstheorie: Evolutionsfaktoren, Artbildung, Koevolution, molekulare Stammbäume und den adaptiven Wert von Verhalten; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Populationsgenetik sowie die Evolution des Menschen und kulturelle Evolution.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is exploring a local ecosystem: measuring environmental factors, identifying plants and invertebrates, and learning about food webs, energy flow, the carbon cycle, climate change and nature conservation.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erkundet ein heimisches Ökosystem: Umweltfaktoren messen, Pflanzen und Wirbellose bestimmen sowie Nahrungsnetze, Energiefluss, Kohlenstoffkreislauf, Klimawandel und Naturschutz verstehen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is analysing ecosystems quantitatively: tolerance curves, ecological niches, predator–prey cycles, the effects of global warming and sustainable ecosystem management; Leistungskurs students also study population growth and the nitrogen cycle.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind analysiert Ökosysteme genauer: Toleranzkurven, ökologische Nische, Räuber-Beute-Beziehungen, Folgen der Erderwärmung und nachhaltiges Ökosystemmanagement; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Populationswachstum und Stickstoffkreislauf.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to plan experiments with hypotheses and control groups and to use and judge models in biology.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, Experimente mit Hypothese und Kontrollansatz zu planen und Modelle in der Biologie zu nutzen und zu beurteilen.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to tell "how" from "why" explanations in biology and to reach reasoned ethical judgements on issues such as organ donation or genetic testing.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, proximate und ultimate Erklärungen zu unterscheiden und sich zu bioethischen Fragen wie Organspende oder Gentests ein begründetes Urteil zu bilden.

clusters.subject: Biologie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is reflecting on how scientific knowledge in biology is produced, tested and revised.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind reflektiert, wie biologisches Wissen gewonnen, überprüft und weiterentwickelt wird.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is starting chemistry: identifying substances by measured properties, sorting mixtures, elements and compounds, separating mixtures, using the particle model and handling chemicals safely.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind beginnt mit Chemie: Stoffe an messbaren Eigenschaften erkennen, Gemische, Elemente und Verbindungen ordnen, Stoffe trennen, das Teilchenmodell nutzen und sicher mit Chemikalien umgehen.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning Dalton's atomic model and how Rutherford discovered the nucleus, with protons, neutrons and electrons.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt das Daltonsche Atommodell kennen und wie Rutherford den Atomkern mit Protonen, Neutronen und Elektronen entdeckte.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning the shell model of the atom and how to use the periodic table to predict the behaviour of elements such as alkali metals and halogens.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt das Schalenmodell und nutzt das Periodensystem, um das Verhalten von Elementen wie Alkalimetallen und Halogenen vorherzusagen.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how atoms bond (ionic, covalent and metallic bonds), how molecules are shaped, and how forces between molecules explain boiling points, solubility and the special properties of water.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Atome Bindungen eingehen (Ionen-, Elektronenpaar- und Metallbindung), wie Moleküle räumlich gebaut sind und wie zwischenmolekulare Kräfte Siedetemperaturen, Löslichkeit und die besonderen Eigenschaften des Wassers erklären.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to recognise chemical reactions, to understand combustion as a reaction with oxygen and the conservation of mass, and to write and balance chemical equations.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, chemische Reaktionen zu erkennen, die Verbrennung als Reaktion mit Sauerstoff und die Massenerhaltung zu verstehen sowie Reaktionsgleichungen aufzustellen.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to count particles with the mole and to calculate amounts and concentrations in chemical reactions.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, mit der Stoffmenge (Mol) zu rechnen und Massen und Konzentrationen bei chemischen Reaktionen zu berechnen.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning that reactions release or absorb energy and why many reactions need a start (activation energy).
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, dass Reaktionen Energie abgeben oder aufnehmen und warum viele Reaktionen erst gestartet werden müssen (Aktivierungsenergie).

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how catalysts speed up reactions, from car exhausts to industry.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Katalysatoren Reaktionen beschleunigen – vom Autokatalysator bis zur Industrie.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is calculating reaction enthalpies, measuring them by calorimetry and using Hess's law; Leistungskurs students also use entropy and free enthalpy to predict whether reactions run by themselves.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind berechnet Reaktionsenthalpien, misst sie kalorimetrisch und wendet den Satz von Hess an; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Entropie und freie Enthalpie.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying how fast reactions run, what equilibrium means, how to shift it (Le Chatelier) and calculate it (law of mass action), with ammonia synthesis as the industrial example; Leistungskurs students also study solubility equilibria.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind untersucht Reaktionsgeschwindigkeit und chemisches Gleichgewicht, das Prinzip von Le Chatelier und das Massenwirkungsgesetz am Beispiel der Ammoniaksynthese; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Löslichkeitsgleichgewichte.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning about acidic and alkaline solutions, the pH scale, neutralisation, acids as proton donors, and how to find a concentration by titration.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt saure und alkalische Lösungen, den pH-Wert, die Neutralisation, Säuren als Protonendonatoren und die Konzentrationsbestimmung durch Titration kennen.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is working with acid constants and pH calculations; Leistungskurs students also calculate pH of weak acids, study buffer systems and interpret titration curves.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind arbeitet mit Säurekonstanten und pH-Berechnungen; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich schwache Säuren, Puffersysteme und Titrationskurven.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning how metals are extracted from their ores by taking away oxygen and how metals differ in how readily they react.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, wie Metalle durch Sauerstoffentzug aus Erzen gewonnen werden und wie sich edle und unedle Metalle unterscheiden.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning redox reactions as electron transfer, how batteries and galvanic cells produce electricity, and how electrolysis works.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt Redoxreaktionen als Elektronenübertragung kennen, wie Batterien und galvanische Elemente Strom liefern und wie eine Elektrolyse funktioniert.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying electrochemistry: oxidation numbers, standard potentials and cell voltages, batteries and fuel cells, electrolysis and corrosion; Leistungskurs students also use the Nernst equation and Faraday's laws.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erarbeitet die Elektrochemie: Oxidationszahlen, Standardpotenziale und Zellspannung, Akkus und Brennstoffzellen, Elektrolyse und Korrosion; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Nernst-Gleichung und Faraday-Gesetze.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is starting organic chemistry with alkanes and alcohols: their names, structures and properties.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind beginnt mit der organischen Chemie: Alkane und Alkohole, ihre Namen, Strukturen und Eigenschaften.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying organic compound classes (aldehydes, carboxylic acids, esters, alkenes) and reaction mechanisms; Leistungskurs students also study nucleophilic substitution, aromatic compounds and chirality.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind erarbeitet organische Stoffklassen (Aldehyde, Carbonsäuren, Ester, Alkene) und Reaktionsmechanismen; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich nucleophile Substitution, Aromaten und Chiralität.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning that plastics are giant molecules and why their structure explains how we use them.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, dass Kunststoffe aus Makromolekülen bestehen und wie ihre Struktur ihre Verwendung erklärt.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager is studying how plastics are made and recycled, and the chemistry of fats and amino acids; Leistungskurs students also study polymerisation mechanisms and carbohydrates.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind untersucht Kunststoffsynthese und -recycling sowie Fette und Aminosäuren; im Leistungskurs zusätzlich Polymerisationsmechanismen und Kohlenhydrate.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning standard tests to identify oxygen, hydrogen, carbon dioxide and water.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt Nachweisreaktionen für Sauerstoff, Wasserstoff, Kohlenstoffdioxid und Wasser.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning to identify ions in salts and mineral water with precipitation reactions and flame tests.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, Ionen in Salzen und Mineralwasser mit Fällungsreaktionen und Flammenfärbung nachzuweisen.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager (in the Leistungskurs) is learning chromatography and instrumental methods such as conductometry and photometry.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt im Leistungskurs Chromatografie und instrumentelle Verfahren wie Konduktometrie und Fotometrie.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is learning why metals are precious resources and why recycling them saves energy and raw materials.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind lernt, warum Metalle wertvolle Rohstoffe sind und warum Recycling Energie und Ressourcen spart.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your child is comparing fossil and renewable fuels and learning how greenhouse gases form and affect the climate.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind vergleicht fossile und regenerative Energieträger und lernt, wie Treibhausgase entstehen und das Klima beeinflussen.

clusters.subject: Chemie
clusters.summary: Your teenager (in the Leistungskurs) is studying nanomaterials and weighing their opportunities and risks.
clusters.summaryDe: Ihr Kind untersucht im Leistungskurs Nanomaterialien und wägt Chancen und Risiken ab.
